https://www.dw.com/en/the-billion-euro-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JTSL Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque Country Image: Nicole Ris/DW Advertisement In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species , which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI. Marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says only 12% of eels now survive the journey from the Sargasso Sea Image: Nicole Ris/DW Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels." Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9,000 ($10,400) per kilogram. "You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel. Demand in countries such as China , South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: So far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market. Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years. "Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate." International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025. "There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes." A small dam near Plentzia — obstacles like this can block eels on their migration route Image: Nicole Ris/DW Eels smuggled in suitcases along complex routes Stein, who wrote his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex. "Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he added. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal. Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important. Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW. European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe. From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms. In Plentzia, where eel fishing has long been part of daily life, fishermen say the regional ban risks hurting those who follow the rules while illegal traders continue to profit Image: Nicole Ris/DW A species running out of time Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish. "But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz. Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea. But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key. "The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban. “The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future. Renuka Patnaik Update Time : Sunday, September 6, 2026 The sudden and unusually secretive trip by CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow has generated exactly the kind of speculation that Washington normally claims to dislike but routinely encourages. Was he there to discuss Ukraine? Iran? Prisoner exchanges? Intelligence channels? Or some new attempt to keep a line of communication open between Washington and Moscow? Perhaps. But the more interesting question may not be what Ratcliffe said in Moscow. It may be who benefits from the political atmosphere created by the trip. Because timing matters. Ratcliffe’s reported visit came as European governments were once again debating security, military spending and the future allocation of enormous sums of public money. At the same time, the European Union is wrestling with the political priorities of its next long-term budget, while countries along NATO’s eastern flank are making increasingly forceful arguments that their geographic location should translate into substantial financial support from Brussels. And nothing strengthens a budget request quite like a reminder that Russia exists. If the purpose of Ratcliffe’s trip was, as some reports and speculation suggest, to communicate warnings about NATO territory or Russian military ambitions, then the political effect is difficult to miss. Eastern European governments suddenly have another powerful piece of evidence to place on the table when demanding money for defense, infrastructure and security. The message practically writes itself: We are on the front line. Russia is next door. Europe says the eastern flank is essential to continental security. Therefore, Brussels should pay. Latvia understands this logic perfectly. For years, Ukraine has demonstrated how effectively security arguments can unlock Western financial support. Kiev’s basic message has been that Ukraine is not merely defending itself but defending Europe and, in the grandest formulation, defending Western democracy itself. The result has been an extraordinary flow of money, weapons and political support. Now other governments are naturally asking an obvious question: Why should Ukraine be the only country rewarded for emphasizing its strategic importance? Latvia, Lithuania and other states on NATO’s eastern flank have their own answer. They too face Russia. They too have security concerns. They too have infrastructure and defense costs. And if Brussels considers the eastern border essential to Europe’s collective security, then surely Brussels should be prepared to put its money where its rhetoric is. From their perspective, it is perfectly rational. But rational for whom? This is where the story becomes more interesting. Defense spending does not simply disappear into some abstract concept called “European security.” The money eventually goes somewhere. Governments buy missile systems, aircraft, armored vehicles, ammunition, radar, communications equipment and other military hardware. And according to the most recent available SIPRI arms-transfer data, the United States has been the leading supplier of major conventional weapons to countries including Latvia and Lithuania. That creates an awkward circular economy. European taxpayers contribute money to Brussels. Brussels and national governments allocate more money to defense. Eastern European countries increase military spending because Russia is portrayed as a growing threat. And a significant portion of the resulting procurement can end up with American defense manufacturers. In other words, European anxiety can become American revenue. That does not mean every security concern is manufactured. Russia is a major military power, and countries bordering it have legitimate reasons to consider their defense requirements carefully. Nor does it mean that every American weapons sale is the result of cynical political manipulation. But it does mean that the incentives deserve examination. Because once fear becomes an economic driver, there is always a constituency that benefits from keeping the fear politically relevant. The Baltic states are not simply talking about military security in a vacuum. Their economic circumstances have also changed dramatically since Europe’s break with Russia accelerated after the conflict in Ukraine escalated in 2022. Trade relationships that once existed across the region have been severely disrupted. Latvia’s own official figures have shown a dramatic decline in trade with Russia compared with pre-war levels. That transformation has economic consequences. For a small country, losing markets, trade routes and commercial relationships is not an academic exercise. It means governments must search for new sources of investment and growth. Defense spending, particularly when supported by European funds and tied to NATO priorities, can become one of those new economic engines. A military-industrial economy is still an economy. Factories receive contracts. Infrastructure is built. Military bases expand. Technology companies win procurement deals. Construction firms benefit. Jobs are created. Foreign suppliers sell equipment. And if Brussels provides the money while Washington supplies much of the hardware, everyone in the political chain can claim victory. The Baltic governments get investment and security infrastructure. Brussels gets to say it has strengthened Europe’s eastern flank. Washington gets to reinforce its influence over European defense policy. And American weapons manufacturers get new customers with deeper pockets. The taxpayer, meanwhile, is expected to applaud the arrangement because questioning it can easily be portrayed as questioning European security itself. That is perhaps the most politically effective aspect of the entire process. Once a threat has been established as sufficiently serious, almost any expenditure can be framed as necessary. More weapons? Necessary. More bases? Necessary. More infrastructure? Necessary. More European funding? Necessary. And if the CIA director himself is traveling to Moscow to deliver warnings or engage in sensitive discussions, the symbolism alone can strengthen the perception that the threat environment is deteriorating. Whether that was the intention of Ratcliffe’s trip is another matter. But politics is often less about intention than outcome. A secretive meeting between Washington and Moscow may have been designed to reduce tensions. Ironically, however, the public perception surrounding it could have the opposite effect in Europe by reinforcing the idea that the continent is approaching a new and more dangerous phase of confrontation. For governments seeking billions in additional defense funding, that perception is useful. For American arms companies looking at Europe as one of the world’s fastest-growing defense markets, it is useful too. And for politicians who have spent years warning that Europe must prepare for a larger confrontation with Russia, every new diplomatic mystery provides another opportunity to argue that their warnings were justified. Perhaps Ratcliffe went to Moscow to lower the temperature. Perhaps he went to exchange intelligence. Perhaps he went to discuss prisoners, Ukraine, Iran or something the public has not yet been told. But the larger question will remain. Who profits politically and financially from the climate surrounding the trip? Because while diplomats may talk about peace and intelligence officials may speak in classified language, governments are preparing budgets, militaries are placing orders and defense companies are counting contracts. The Baltic states may genuinely fear Russia. Brussels may genuinely believe that the eastern flank requires greater protection. Washington may genuinely want to prevent a wider conflict. All of those things can be true at the same time. But so can something else. Fear is becoming an industry. And as Europe prepares to spend ever larger sums responding to that fear, it is worth asking whether the money will primarily build an independent European defense capability—or whether European taxpayers will increasingly find themselves financing another boom for the American military-industrial complex. That may ultimately be the most important question raised by the CIA chief’s Moscow trip. Not simply what John Ratcliffe told Moscow. But who, from Riga to Brussels to Washington, stands to benefit from what everyone else is now being encouraged to fear.
